   Cheap pizza is one. Casey’s large pie costs $13.99, which is some 22% below comparable pizza offerings, according to a report from William Blair. Domino’s, Papa Johns and Pizza Hut’s pizzas are all priced closer to $20, for example.

   Casey’s cheaper offering is speaking to inflation-weary consumers. Its same-store sales growth of prepared food and dispensed beverages has exceeded those of Domino’s U.S. in 18 out of the last 20 quarters, according to data from Wells Fargo. 

   How is it able to sell on the cheap? Casey’s sells more stuff under one roof—including groceries, fuel and tobacco. So it distributes labor and fixed costs across more revenue. Stores are all owned and operated by Casey’s, not franchised, which means no royalty or franchise fees. 

   Plus, surging labor and input costs have left mom-and-pop convenience stores with no choice but to raise fuel prices to compensate. That in turn helps larger chains like Casey’s improve their fuel margins, too, giving them some room to keep pizza prices ultra competitive, notes Phillip Blee, equity analyst at William Blair. 

   Casey’s booming pizza business and acquisitions have helped the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization expand at a compound annual growth rate of 16% over the last three fiscal years. Mighty Costco’s Ebitda has grown at a more moderate 9.3% rate over an equivalent period. Casey’s has also been a good steward of capital with returns on invested capital close to 10% or higher over the last seven fiscal years.

   Casey’s has scale in an otherwise fragmented convenience-store industry. About 63% of all convenience stores are owned by an entity that has 10 or fewer stores, according to NACS, a trade association. That gives the company plenty of room to keep growing through acquisitions.

   New menu items are another potential driver. It is just starting to roll out a wings business that it expects to reach all its stores over the next two years. About half of Casey’s stores don’t have a national pizza or wing chain competitor within five miles, the company said at its investor day earlier this year. 

   Casey’s still has plenty of gas left in its tank.

The new pizza wars

 

With the Iran war dragging on, consumer sentiment weak and periodic jitters around AI stocks, a defensive consumer stock might be just what investors are craving.
